# Obfuscated Code

Code clarity is a security concern, not just a style preference.

Reviewers, maintainers, and auditors rely on code being readable enough to
understand what it actually does. When code is misleading, visually deceptive,
or dependent on surprising language rules, defects are easier to hide and
security review becomes less reliable.

This example is a collection of small Java puzzlers. Each one is intentionally
short so the lesson stays focused on a single source of confusion.

## What you will learn

By the end of this example you will understand:

- why visually clever code is risky even when it is technically valid Java
- how autoboxing, numeric promotion, and compound assignment can hide
  surprising behavior
- how Unicode identifiers can make code look clearer than it really is
- why secure coding depends on reviewable, explicit code rather than
  puzzle-like shortcuts

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 21 or newer](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java21)

## Build the example

Build the project once before running the puzzlers.

We do this first so all example classes are compiled into `target/classes`,
which lets us run each example individually without rebuilding between steps.

What you gain from this step: a repeatable baseline for the rest of the
walkthrough.

```shell
./mvnw clean compile
```

## Example 1: autoboxing and cached Integers

Before running this example, try to predict the output.

The code compares boxed `Integer` values using `==` instead of `.equals()`. That
looks harmless, but `==` checks object identity, not value equality.

What you gain from this step: you see why code that appears to compare numbers
can actually be comparing object references.

```java
package com.oracle.jsc.obfuscated;

public final class Example01 {

    public static void main(final String[] args) {
        final Integer a = 42;
        final Integer b = 42;
        System.out.println(a == b);

        final Integer c = 666;
        final Integer d = 666;
        System.out.println(c == d);
    }
}
```

```shell
java --class-path 'target/classes' com.oracle.jsc.obfuscated.Example01
```

Observed output

```
true
false
```

The output is:

- `true` for `42`
- `false` for `666`

Why? Java autoboxing uses `Integer.valueOf()`. The JVM caches commonly used
`Integer` instances in a small range, so the two boxed `42` values refer to the
same cached object. The two boxed `666` values do not.

The secure-coding lesson is straightforward: avoid clever reliance on runtime
caching behavior, and never use `==` when you mean value equality for boxed
numbers.

## Example 2: `char`, arithmetic, and silent narrowing

This example looks like it should keep the character unchanged. It does not.

What you gain from this step: you see how compound assignment can hide numeric
conversion and narrowing in a way that is easy to misread during review.

```java
package com.oracle.jsc.obfuscated;

public final class Example02 {

    public static void main(final String[] args) {
        char ch = '0';
        ch *= 1.1;
        System.out.println(ch);
    }
}
```

```shell
java --class-path 'target/classes' com.oracle.jsc.obfuscated.Example02
```

Observed output

```
4
```

The output is `4`, not `0`.

The variable starts as the character `'0'`, whose numeric code point is `48`.
Multiplying by `1.1` produces `52.8`, and the compound assignment narrows that
result back into `char`, leaving `52`, which is the character `'4'`.

The lesson is that compact syntax can hide conversions. If a conversion matters
to correctness, write it explicitly so the reader does not have to
reverse-engineer the compiler's rules.

## Example 3: Unicode confusable identifiers

This example compiles cleanly, but it is still deceptive.

At a glance, the variable names appear to be the same word with tiny formatting
differences. In reality they are different identifiers because some letters come
from different Unicode alphabets.

What you gain from this step: you see that code can be visually misleading even
when the compiler accepts it without complaint.

```java
package com.oracle.jsc.obfuscated;

public final class Example03 {

    public static void main(final String[] args) {
        final String payload = "Hello ";
        final String paylоad = "World";
        final String payloaԁ = " !!";
        System.out.println(payload + paylоad + payloaԁ);
    }
}
```

```shell
java --class-path 'target/classes' com.oracle.jsc.obfuscated.Example03
```

Observed output

```
Hello World !!
```

The output is `Hello World !!`.

The important detail is not the output itself. It is that the identifiers are
intentionally confusing:

- `payload` uses ordinary Latin letters
- `paylоad` uses a Cyrillic `о`
- `payloaԁ` uses a different Unicode character `ԁ` that looks like `d`

To a hurried reviewer, those names may look identical enough to miss. This is
exactly why obfuscated naming is dangerous: it weakens review, code search, and
maintenance.

## Example 4: compound assignment and floating-point precision

This example is a good reminder that compact expressions can hide both
evaluation order and type conversion.

What you gain from this step: you see how `+=` can introduce a cast and a
precision loss that would be much more obvious if written out longhand.

```java
package com.oracle.jsc.obfuscated;

public final class Example04 {

    public static void main(final String[] args) {
        long x = (1 << 24) + 1;
        if (x != (x += 0.0f)) {
            System.out.println("What??");
        } else {
            System.out.println("OK!");
        }
        System.out.println("x = " + x + "; ... (x += 0.0f) = " + (x += 0.0f));
    }
}
```

```shell
java --class-path 'target/classes' com.oracle.jsc.obfuscated.Example04
```

Observed output

```
What??
x = 16777216; ... (x += 0.0f) = 16777216
```

The output is:

- `What??`
- `x = 16777216; ... (x += 0.0f) = 16777216`

Even though `0.0f` looks like it should change nothing, `x += 0.0f` is
effectively evaluated as:

```java
x = (long) ((float) x + 0.0f);
```

The intermediate `float` cannot represent `16777217` exactly, so the value
is rounded down to `16777216` before being cast back.

The secure-coding lesson is to avoid dense expressions that hide narrowing and
precision loss. If an expression depends on exact numeric behavior, spell the
steps out clearly.

## BigCharacters: bidi controls and misleading source layout

This final example looks odd even before you run it.

What you gain from this step: you see that source code can be made visually
misleading by Unicode directionality controls, not just by odd naming.

```java
package com.oracle.jsc.obfuscated;
import static java.lang.Character.getNumericValue;

public final class BigCharacters {

    public static void main(final String...a‮) {
        for (char c‮ = 1; c‮ > 0; c‮++)
            if (getNumericValue(c‮) > 50)
                System.out.println(c‮ + ": " + getNumericValue(c‮));
    }
}
```

```shell
java --class-path 'target/classes' com.oracle.jsc.obfuscated.BigCharacters
```

Observed output

```
௱: 100
௲: 1000
൱: 100
൲: 1000
፷: 60
፸: 70
፹: 80
፺: 90
፻: 100
፼: 10000
Ⅽ: 100
Ⅾ: 500
Ⅿ: 1000
ⅽ: 100
ⅾ: 500
ⅿ: 1000
ↀ: 1000
ↁ: 5000
ↂ: 10000
ↇ: 50000
ↈ: 100000
㉍: 60
㉎: 70
㉏: 80
```

The program prints Unicode characters whose numeric values are greater than
`50`.

The trick is in the identifier spelling. The parameter and loop variable contain
a bidirectional control character, which changes how parts of the source are
displayed to a human reader. The code is valid, but it is much harder to review
safely because what you see is not an honest, straightforward representation of
the underlying token sequence.

This is exactly the kind of thing a secure-coding workshop should call out: if
code requires a puzzle-solving mindset to read, it is already too risky.

## What this example teaches

- Readability is part of security because unreadable code is harder to review correctly.
- Avoid relying on surprising language features to save a line or look clever.
- Use explicit comparisons, conversions, and names so the code says what it means.
- Treat visually deceptive Unicode usage as a real review and maintenance risk, not as a curiosity.
